lesson.title: DC Coupling: Seeing the Whole Signal, Offset Included
lesson.summary: DC coupling connects the oscilloscope input directly to the signal with no blocking capacitor, so the trace shows the true instantaneous voltage, constant offset and all, making it the right choice whenever the actual DC level matters.
lesson.body:
The other coupling option on an oscilloscope input is DC coupling, and it is in most respects the simpler of the two: there is no series capacitor at all, the probe tip connects directly through to the scope's input resistance and vertical amplifier. Whatever voltage is actually present at the probe tip at a given instant, DC offset and all, is exactly what gets displayed. Nothing is filtered out and nothing is blocked.

As the previous chapter on AC coupling showed, that direct connection is precisely what AC coupling gives up in exchange for zooming in on a small ripple. DC coupling is the right choice whenever you actually need to know the absolute voltage level, not just how it is wiggling. A good example is checking the logic levels on a digital circuit. If you want to confirm that a signal claiming to be a logic high is really sitting near 5 volts, or 3.3 volts, and not drooping down to 2 volts due to a loading problem or a weak driver, you need DC coupling, because AC coupling would strip away that offset and simply recenter the square wave around zero volts on the screen, making a healthy 5 volt logic high look identical to a badly drooping 3 volt one.

The same logic applies to any circuit where the DC operating point itself is the thing under test: checking that a voltage divider is really producing the resistor ratio you calculated, checking that a power supply rail is actually at its rated voltage, or checking the bias point of a transistor or op amp stage before worrying about how any AC signal riding on top of it behaves. In all of these situations, throwing away the DC information, which is exactly what AC coupling does, would throw away the very thing you are trying to measure.

Because most day to day probing is about confirming that a circuit's DC levels are correct, DC coupling is the default setting on most oscilloscopes, and the one you should reach for first unless you have a specific reason, like a small ripple sitting on a large DC rail, to switch to AC coupling instead. A good habit is to start any new measurement in DC coupled mode to see the whole picture, offset and all, and only switch to AC coupling once you have identified a small detail that the DC offset is making hard to see.
